newsitem.title: GREECE: OLYMPICS-ATHENS WANTS 2004 GAMES BUT CAN IT AFFORD THEM?.
newsitem.headline: OLYMPICS-ATHENS WANTS 2004 GAMES BUT CAN IT AFFORD THEM?.

text.p: Athens has put together an impressive bidding dossier for the 2004 Olympic Games but concern over the cost of hosting the giant sports festival is giving many government officials cold feet.

"A number of senior advisers inside the government say we can't afford the Olympics," a government official told Reuters. "But there is strong public support to bring the Games to Greece and if Athens wins them it will be a race to raise cash."
According to the bidding dossier obtained by Reuters, Greece will spend some $1.6 billion if Athens wins the 2004 Olympics and expects a profit of $36.6 million at the end of the event.

The only certain revenue at this point is the allocation of about $700 million by the International Olympic Committee (IOC) to the host city. Television rights are expected to yield some $600 million and the remainder will come from ticket sales, lotteries and sponsors.
"These figures match up on paper but those who warn about the cost say it may rise by another billion dollars by 2004. This is alot of money for a country like Greece," the government official said.

Greeks are already hard pressed to meet the requirements of the European Monetary Union by the year 2000 and the government was expected to abolish a series of tax breaks next year which will yield some $1.8 billion to finance towering state debts.

The government also plans to spend some $3 billion in the next four years for buying new weapons to counter perceived threats by rival Turkey and Prime Minister Costas Simitis has said he may resort to foreign borrowing to come up with the sum.
"We constantly ask Greeks to pay more and I don't know if the current enthusiasm to host the Olympics will continue when the Olympic bills must be paid," the official said.
A recent nationwide poll by the bidding committee showed that 96.4 percent of Greeks want the Olympics and thousands have already signed up as volunteers.

"There is no other (bidding) city which expects your decision with such suspense," President Costis Stephanopoulos told Thomas Bach, president of the IOC's evaluation commission visiting Athens for an on-site inspection.
The commission met on Thursday with Simitis who assured them that the state would cover the cost of the Olympics.
Greece fought hard to stage the centennial Olympics this year, saying it had a special right as the country where the ancient Games originated and where they were revived in 1896.
But the IOC voted down the bid because of Greece's poor infrastructure and a lack of confidence that Athens could meet the demands of the Olympic Games.

"This is a totally new bid with a totally new attitude," said bidding committee head Yanna Angelopoulou. "Eighty percent of the sports facilities are already in place and we have the money for the rest. We are proud of our Olympic heritage but we don't depend on it to win the Games."
Angelopoulou said all 11 cities bidding for the 2004 Games were strong candidates but other bidding committee officials said they saw Athens, Rome and Stockholm as favourites.
Bach said Athens will be tested next August when it hosts the world Athletics championships.
"Our (evaluation) report will be in February but for the final decision the world championships will be a showcase for Athens," he said.
The IOC will vote on the host city for the 2004 Olympics at a meeting in Lausanne, Switzerland, next September.
